title: Jacob and Esau: Not Arbitrary Choice
english: “…having conceived by our father Isaac” (Romans 9:10).

One should note that the aim of this sentence is by no means brought to completion; rather it is left hanging and needs a brief addition, that is, words to be understood, so that it may not appear to limp.
What I mean is this.

He had already shown, from the fact that Isaac was given to Abraham by promise, that the children of the flesh would not necessarily be counted to him as offspring, and that it would rather befit him to bear the name of father of those who are of faith and promise.

Then he takes up Rebecca and what happened in her case, and says, “And not only so,” that is, my argument will not stop at the birth of Isaac alone, “but also Rebecca, having conceived by one, our father Isaac” (Romans 9:10).

And he needed to add something like this: “will also be brought in as proof and assurance,” that is, “will serve as a pattern and image of the calling and grace that come by election and foreknowledge.”
For had something of that kind been added, his sentence would then have seemed complete.
But I do not know how he came to pass this over and go straight on to what was said and done at the birth of Isaac’s sons.
“What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means” (Romans 9:14), and so on, down to “he called us, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles” (Romans 9:24).

It was likely that some fault-finders would suppose that Jacob and Esau had met with an untested swing of will, and that the one was loved because God nodded assent out of personal favour, while the other was hated (Romans 9:13).

So the apostle of necessity does away in advance with this view of the matter as ruinous, and tries to speak in defence of the decrees from above, setting against his own words, as it were, what seems to oppose them.

For if, he says, even before the infants had done anything, before any testing of them and before any deeds, the one was thought worthy of love and the other was hated, and was even appointed to serve the younger (Romans 9:11–12), then perhaps, he says, God is even unjust.
And then how is this not senseless?

For if Jacob had not become a good man, if Esau had not been wicked, one might reasonably say that the foreknowledge had perhaps gone astray, and that what was determined for both of them was the work of a random impulse and an unsteady will.

But since Esau was very perverse and Jacob wise, God’s foreknowledge would do no wrong at all in granting, even ahead of time, to the one who was good in his ways that he should be loved, and to the one who was not such that he should be condemned.
For it would have been no hard thing for God to bear with them patiently and wait for the time of their deeds, so that each might be shown plainly by his own actions.

But since the mystery of grace by election and of the gift given in foreknowledge had to be sketched out beforehand, for that very reason God, our supreme craftsman in such things, put the moment to good use and all but seized it.

At the birth of the children he assured Isaac that, though he was the one and only son from Abraham, he would be the father of countless nations, those who are of the promise and who would be called in faith.
But if, in keeping with…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf), PG columns 226–227.
The row opens inside the Romans 9:10 lemma that u08-open cut at ἐξ ἑνός; the English supplies 'having conceived by our father Isaac' from κοίτην ἔχουσα Ἰσαὰκ τοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν only.
The row ends mid-sentence at εἰ δὲ δὴ κατὰ; the object γνῶσιν heads u08-rem-mid. The English keeps the cut ('But if, in keeping with…') and adds nothing.
Inline page number 22 and PG column 227 are print markers and are left out of the English.

Cyril's grammatical remark: Paul's 'not only so, but also Rebecca …' (Romans 9:10) lacks a main verb. Cyril supplies the kind of words that would complete it, and they are given in quotation marks as his own suggestion, not as Scripture.

ῥοπῆς θελημάτων ἀβασανίστου: 'an untested leaning of wills', i.e. a choice made without any weighing of merit; rendered 'an untested swing of will'. ἰδίᾳ χάριτι κατανεύοντος τοῦ Θεοῦ: 'God nodding assent out of personal favour', i.e. favouritism, which the objectors allege.

The sentence 'For if, he says, even before the infants … God is unjust as well' voices the objection Paul raises against himself; Cyril then calls it senseless (ἀπόπληκτον). The voices are kept distinct: the objection is not Cyril's view.
σκαιός: literally 'left-handed', hence 'awkward, perverse'; set against σοφός ('wise').
προανατυποῦσθαι: 'to be prefigured, outlined beforehand'; rendered 'sketched out beforehand'.
ἀριστοτέχνας: 'supreme craftsman', an epithet of God as maker; kept.
ὡς ἐν πίστει κληθησομένων: 'as those to be called in faith'; rendered 'who would be called in faith'.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u08 rem early

title: Who Are You to Answer God?
english: …knowledge, he, as God, again has pity on those he may choose, or rather on those to whom it is fitting that mercy be shown, for he said somewhere to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15), then how will the matter not be beyond all reproach?
The apostle, I think, clearly foresaw that some would perhaps suppose that it is by God’s nod that some are good and others disobedient.

So of necessity he himself puts forward the objection that springs from their ignorance, and says, “So then it depends not on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16).

For if Esau was hated even before he had done anything wicked, and Jacob was honoured even before he came into being, and if again God has mercy on whom he has mercy, is it not then right to conclude that the one who runs or wills, that is, the one eager to do something good, gains nothing, and that everything about us hangs on the nods of God?

Then he heaps on top of these the words that could fix that opinion still more firmly, and says, “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you’” (Romans 9:17; Exodus 9:16).
To these he adds what is, as it were, the conclusion of the whole problem, and says, “So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18).
“You will say to me then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?’” (Romans 9:19).
What, then, was his way of answering?
It is very obscure, and perhaps even seems to support the objections they raise; yet it is enough to assure us that nothing could come from God that lies outside what is fitting.
For he gives to each what befits him: he pities and has mercy on those for whom mercy is fitting, and he subjects the wicked to punishment.
Yet his wrath does not follow the offences at once and on their heels; rather, a long patience goes before it, so that some even suppose that God has stopped caring about those on earth.
So Paul brings out his reply and stands up to those who say such things, directing the force of his words at the persons who had been brought forward, I mean Esau and also Pharaoh.

He spoke, then, as though to each of those he had named: “But who indeed are you, O man, to answer back to God? Will what is moulded say to the one who moulded it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” (Romans 9:20).
For he shows, as from a plain example, that it is a very grave thing to find fault with God’s judgments.

For if anyone chooses to think as he ought, he will leave to God, who knows all things, the judging of each matter in whatever way God himself knows, and he will not doubt in the least that whatever God chooses to do is holy, as he shapes with full authority whatever concerns each one.
So he sharply blames those who bring a probing mind to bear at all on God’s decrees, as to whether they are right or not.

For they ought, he says, rather to imitate what is moulded by the potter’s hand, and to bear in silence what comes from God, for “what is moulded will not say to the one who moulded it, ‘Why have you made me like this?’” (Romans 9:20).
But perhaps some say this in reply as well: “If…”
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf), PG columns 227–229.

The row opens mid-sentence: u08-rem-early ends εἰ δὲ δὴ κατὰ, and this row begins γνῶσιν. The English resumes '…knowledge' (completing 'in keeping with' at the end of u08-rem-early) and keeps ὡς Θεός as 'he, as God'; 'then' marks the apodosis πῶς οὐχ … ἔσται.
The row ends at Εἰ, the first word of an objection that continues in u08-rem-close; the English keeps the cut ('If…').
Inline PG column numbers 228 and 229 and page number 23 are print markers and are left out of the English.

The question 'is it not then right to conclude … hangs on the nods of God?' states the inference of those who misread Paul; Cyril's own answer follows from 'What, then, was his way of answering?' The voices are kept distinct.
νεύματα: 'nods', i.e. bare decrees of God's will; kept as 'nod/nods' to preserve Cyril's image.
ἀφειδῆσαι τῶν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς: LSJ ἀφειδέω with genitive 'to disregard, neglect'; rendered 'has stopped caring about those on earth'.

τοῦ λόγου τὴν δύναμιν ἐπαφεὶς τῷ προσώπῳ τῶν παρενηνεγμένων: 'directing the force of his words at the persons who had been brought forward'; Cyril reads Romans 9:20 as addressed to the figures of Esau and Pharaoh.
ἀλιτήριος: 'sinner, guilty wretch'; rendered 'the wicked'.
παγχάλεπον: 'very hard, very grievous'; rendered 'a very grave thing'.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u08 rem mid

title: Vessels Made by Their Own Choices
english: “…like a potter, God moulds in whatever way he wishes, so as to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour (Romans 9:21), how will reason not persuade anyone at all to think that whatever has come to be is in every way and wholly just as it was made? So one person has come into being for dishonour and has been allotted a nature of that kind, while another has been made, or rather raised up, hard, so that, as he himself says, his name may be proclaimed in all the earth (Exodus 9:16; Romans 9:17). What charge, then, can still be brought against those who fall? For they were made for this.”

To such arguments one might reply, first of all, that they could not claim that the force of these thoughts hints to us at differences of nature. For he did not say that some were made harsh and hardened, or made into vessels of honour and of dishonour, nor did he assign them such a nature at all. Rather, he leads us to think this: that some are moulded like vessels of clay, some for honour and some for dishonour; and we have been taught the meaning of the illustration from the words of the prophets. In what way, then, some are moulded as if by a potter, some for honour and others for dishonour, and for what causes, anyone may learn by reading the words of Jeremiah. It is written thus:

“Arise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear my words. And I went down to the potter’s house, and there he was, making a piece of work on the stones. And the vessel that he was making fell in his hands; and again he made it into another vessel, as it seemed good in his sight to make it. And the word of the Lord came,” he says, “to me, saying: Shall I not be able to make you as this potter does, house of Israel? Look, like the potter’s clay, you are in my hands. At last I will speak against a nation or against a kingdom, to root them out; and that nation will turn from all its evils, and I will relent concerning the evils that I planned to do to them. And at last I will speak concerning a nation and concerning a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it; and they will do evil before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will relent concerning the good things that I said I would do for them” (Jeremiah 18:2–10).

Do you see how some are moulded for honour and for dishonour, not because they were allotted a nature made that way, but because they receive an equal and fitting return for what they do? So if the Maker of all punishes the one who passes from good ways to more shameful ones, and crowns with honours the one who moves from the more shameful to the better, how is it not true to say that some have by no means become evil by nature, or been moulded so by him, but have rather become vessels of dishonour because, though it was open to them to choose to win approval with God, they fell sick with a willing inclination toward evil? But…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

Section opens mid-sentence: u08-rem-mid ends with the objection's first word Εἰ ('If…'), opened there with a quotation mark; this row continues the objection with a leading ellipsis and closes the quotation at γεγόνασι γὰρ εἰς τοῦτο ('For they were made for this').
ἁπαστισοῦν: run-together form in the edition, read as ἅπαντα τινὰ οὖν / ἁπαντασοῦν, 'anyone at all'.

ἡ γραφή in ποία… ἔτι τοῖς πταίουσιν ἡ γραφή is the legal sense 'indictment, charge', not 'Scripture'; rendered 'What charge… can still be brought'. The same sense is kept for γραφῆς… τῆς ἐν νόμῳ in u09-rem-mid.
διαπλάττω / πλάττομαι: 'mould', matching 'moulded by the potter’s hand' in u08-rem-mid.
μετανοήσω (LXX, of God): rendered 'I will relent', the standard sense when God is the subject; literally 'I will repent'.
ἐπὶ τῶν λίθων (LXX): 'on the stones', kept as Cyril quotes it (the potter's wheel); πέρας (LXX): 'at last'.

ἐθελούσιον ἠῤῥωστήκασι τὴν εἰς τὰ φαῦλα ῥοπήν: accusative of respect, 'they fell sick with a willing inclination toward evil'. Cyril's point is that the inclination is chosen (ἐθελούσιον), not given by nature.
Page numbers 230 and 231 and the footer numeral '24' are edition apparatus and are omitted.
Section ends at Ἀλλ' ('But…'); the objection continues at the start of u09-open (ἐσκλήρυνεν αὐτὸς, φησὶ…).
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos u08 rem close
